title: ConfigureAwait and SynchronizationContext (where await resumes)
hook: await captures a context if one exists. In UI apps that context is the UI thread. In ASP.NET Core and background workers, it usually is not — but libraries you share still need ConfigureAwait(false).

blocks.text: SynchronizationContext is a hook that says 'resume this continuation here.' WinForms and WPF install one so that after an HTTP await you can touch a control on the UI thread. Classic ASP.NET (not Core) had one that re-entered the request. ASP.NET Core and generic hosts do not install a request SynchronizationContext — continuations run on thread-pool threads. ConfigureAwait(false) means: do not marshal back; run the continuation on the completing thread (typically the pool). ConfigureAwait(true) is the default for a naked await.

entries.plainDefinition: A mechanism that determines which thread runs a continuation after await.
entries.example: WPF's DispatcherSynchronizationContext posts back to the UI thread.

entries.plainDefinition: Tells await not to capture the current SynchronizationContext. Continuation runs on any pool thread.
The default behavior: await remembers the current SynchronizationContext and resumes on it.
entries.example: In WinForms, await resumes on the UI thread so you can update controls.

entries.plainDefinition: A thread blocked in .Result waiting for a continuation that needs the same thread to run.
entries.example: UI thread calls .Result on a Task whose continuation needs the UI thread.

blocks.text: The textbook deadlock: a UI or classic ASP.NET thread calls .Result on a Task whose continuation needs that same context to finish. The thread is blocked in Result; the continuation never runs. ASP.NET Core does not have that deadlock, which is why 'we never ConfigureAwait' is a common but incomplete answer. Reusable libraries targeting both UI and servers should ConfigureAwait(false) after every await that does not need the caller's context.

blocks.title: Interview answer template
blocks.body: Say: 'Core apps have no sync context, so blocking is still a scalability bug, not that classic deadlock. Libraries targeting both UI and servers should ConfigureAwait(false) unless they must return to the caller's context.'

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Check for SynchronizationContext
items.body: At each await, the runtime checks if a SynchronizationContext is installed.

items.title: Default (ConfigureAwait true)
items.body: If a context exists, post the continuation to it. UI thread, legacy ASP.NET request thread.

items.title: ConfigureAwait(false)
items.body: Skip context capture. Run the continuation on the thread that completed the I/O.

items.title: No context (ASP.NET Core)
items.body: Both paths behave the same — continuations run on pool threads regardless.

diagram.title: ConfigureAwait decision

snippet.label: Library Redis helper without capturing context
snippet.explanation: A reusable helper must not resume on a captured UI or legacy ASP.NET context. The worker and Kestrel hosts already have none.

snippet.label: Classic deadlock pattern
snippet.explanation: The UI thread is blocked in .Result. The continuation needs the UI thread. Neither can proceed. Fix: await instead of .Result, or ConfigureAwait(false) in the library.

snippet.label: Capture values before ConfigureAwait(false)
snippet.explanation: After ConfigureAwait(false), you may be on a different thread. Capture ambient state (HttpContext values) before the await.

blocks.title: Thread resumption models
rows: Can resume on a different pool thread
Microtasks always on the same JS thread
No deadlock — but blocking blocks the loop

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Claiming ConfigureAwait(false) is required in every ASP.NET Core controller method. Using .Result in a library that later gets called from WinForms, recreating the classic deadlock. Capturing HttpContext after ConfigureAwait(false) and assuming you are still on the request thread. Sprinkling ConfigureAwait in application code without understanding why.

interviewTakeaways: SynchronizationContext, if present, is where await resumes by default.
ASP.NET Core has no request SynchronizationContext; blocking is still wrong.
Reusable libraries should ConfigureAwait(false) unless they must return to the caller's context.
commonPitfalls: Claiming ConfigureAwait(false) is required in every ASP.NET Core controller method.
Using .Result in a library that later gets called from WinForms, recreating the classic deadlock.
Capturing HttpContext after ConfigureAwait(false) and assuming you are still on the request thread (you need to capture values first).

jsTsCorrelations.concept: Microtasks always resume on the same JS thread
jsTsCorrelations.note: There is no ConfigureAwait in the browser: a Promise continuation is a microtask on the same event loop. C# can hop threads; JS cannot hop the JS thread without workers.
